extracted.intended_audience: sellers using negative-option features, corporate compliance officers, consumer-protection lawyers, policymakers, and stakeholders participating in FTC rulemaking or seeking to comply with 16 CFR part 425
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for designing, marketing, disclosing, obtaining consent for, and providing cancellation for negative-option programs (recurring subscriptions and similar features) to comply with the FTC's final Negative Option Rule (16 CFR part 425).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on material misrepresentations (§425.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines as unfair or deceptive the act "to misrepresent any material fact made while marketing using a negative option feature (§ 425.3)".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rule treats any material misrepresentation made while marketing using a negative option feature as an unfair or deceptive practice under section 5 of the FTC Act. The SBP explains that misrepresentations induce consumers to enroll in negative option programs and are a central source of consumer harm (e.g., misstatements about free trials, prices, cancellation rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide important information before obtaining billing information (§425.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires sellers to "provide important information prior to obtaining consumers' billing information in connection with a negative option feature (§ 425.4)".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important information must be provided prior to obtaining billing information and charging consumers. Consistent guidance (and ROSCA/FTC precedent) identifies at minimum: disclosure of the existence of the negative option, the offer's total cost, transfer of a consumer's billing information to a third party (if applicable), and how to cancel the offer. Disclosures must be clear and conspicuous and occur before consumers agree to the purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain express informed consent before charging (§425.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires sellers to "obtain consumers' unambiguously affirmative consent to the negative option feature prior to charging them" (express informed consent) (§ 425.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent must be unambiguous and affirmative (express informed consent), and sellers should obtain acceptance of the negative option feature separately from other portions of the transaction. Billing a consumer without express informed consent is described as an unfair act under section 5 of the FTC Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple cancellation mechanism; immediately halt charges (§425.6, 'Click to Cancel')
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires sellers to "provide a simple mechanism to cancel the negative option feature and immediately halt charges" (§ 425.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanism must be simple and must immediately stop recurring charges. The rule requires cancellation mechanisms to be at least as simple to use as the method the consumer used to initiate the negative option. The SBP breaks down § 425.6 into: (a)-(b) simple mechanism required and parity with initiation; (c) minimum requirements for simple mechanisms (online, telephone, in-person); and (d) 'saves' (retention attempts). The SBP analyzes online cancellation (§ 425.6(c)(1)), telephone cancellation (§ 425.6(c)(2)), and in-person cancellation (§ 425.6(c)(3)), and addresses how 'saves' are handled in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum online, telephone, and in-person cancellation requirements (§425.6(c)(1)-(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifies minimum requirements for simple mechanisms by medium: online cancellation, telephone cancellation, and in-person cancellation (§ 425.6(c)(1)-(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SBP contains separate summaries and analyses for each medium. For online cancellation, requirements focus on unobstructed, direct online methods; for telephone, requirements focus on how calls are handled and whether automated systems create obstacles; for in-person, requirements consider what constitutes a simple, immediate mechanism. The Commission analyzes comments and provides detail in each subpart of the rule's section-by-section analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not impede promised cancellation procedures; honor cancellation requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketers must not impede the effective operation of promised cancellation procedures and must honor cancellation requests that comply with those procedures (one of the six section 5 principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FTC's enforcement practice and the SBP emphasize that sellers cannot create barriers (e.g., multi-step upsells, requiring different or harder methods than enrollment) that prevent consumers from cancelling. Examples of harmful practices include requiring consumers to navigate many 'saves' or use a more difficult method to cancel than to enroll.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5's six basic requirements for negative option marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: FTC case law and guidance identify six basic requirements negative option marketing must follow to avoid deceptive or unfair practices: (1) disclose material terms (including existence of negative option, total cost, transfer of billing info, how to cancel), (2) disclosures must be clear and conspicuous, (3) disclose material terms before consumers agree to the purchase, (4) obtain consumers' consent, (5) do not impede cancellation and honor cancellation requests, and (6) make no material misrepresentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These six requirements are repeatedly cited as the core standards the Final Rule builds on. They apply across media per FTC guidance and are used to evaluate compliance under Section 5 as well as under the new Rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROSCA requirements (online negative option transactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under ROSCA, it is prohibited to charge consumers through an online negative option unless the marketer: (1) clearly and conspicuously discloses all material terms before obtaining billing information, (2) obtains express informed consent before charging, and (3) provides simple mechanisms to stop recurring charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ROSCA applies specifically to online transactions and does not prescribe exact steps to comply; it provides the baseline obligations that the FTC's Rule expands upon for all media. Violations of ROSCA are treated as violations of an FTC trade regulation rule and can result in civil penalties and other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) telephonic disclosure and payment requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For telemarketing negative option offers, the TSR requires disclosure of all material terms, including the need for affirmative consumer action to avoid charges, the date(s) charges will be submitted for payment, and specific steps the customer must take to avoid charges; it also prohibits misrepresentations and contains payment-authorization requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSR requirements are specific to telephone telemarketing and include additional payment authorization rules. The Final Rule expands coverage beyond telephone to all media, but telephonic requirements remain applicable where telemarketing is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: EFTA: written authorization for recurring debit/bank charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act (EFTA), sellers may not impose recurring charges on a consumer's debit cards or bank accounts without written authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EFTA enforces limits on payment-authorizations for debit/bank accounts and supplements disclosure/consent requirements when those payment methods are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unordered Merchandise Statute (mailing unordered goods/bills considered unfair)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unordered Merchandise Statute provides that mailing unordered merchandise, or a bill for such merchandise, constitutes an unfair trade practice in violation of section 5 of the FTC Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute is relevant to negative option practices that send goods or bills to consumers who did not consent; it reinforces expectations around consent and returns/refunds for mailed goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: Final Rule applies to all negative option programs in any media (16 CFR part 425)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule now applies to all negative option programs in any media, expanding beyond the prior Rule that covered only prenotification plans for the sale of goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SBP explains negative option program categories (prenotification plans, continuity plans, automatic renewals, free-to-pay conversions) and states the Final Rule's coverage is across media (telephone, internet, print, in-person). The Rule defines 'negative option seller' and explains how different practices fall within scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure specificity: disclose all material terms necessary to prevent deception (regardless of relation to negative option)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent with ROSCA and the Commission's Enforcement Policy Statement, sellers must "clearly and conspicuously disclose all material terms of the transaction before obtaining the consumer's billing information, regardless of whether a material term directly relates to the terms of the negative option offer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Rule and prior guidance emphasize that omissions about related terms of the underlying product/service can be deceptive even if they don't directly alter the negative option's mechanics (e.g., fees, return costs). The Commission stresses breadth to avoid consumer deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1973 prenotification-plan disclosure list (historical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1973 Rule required prenotification plan sellers to disclose seven material terms: (1) how subscribers must notify the seller if they do not wish to purchase the selection; (2) any minimum purchase obligations; (3) the subscribers' right to cancel; (4) whether billing charges include postage and handling; (5) that subscribers have at least ten days to reject a selection; (6) that if any subscriber is not given ten days to reject a selection, the seller will credit return-of-selection and postage, along with shipping and handling; and (7) the frequency with which announcements and forms will be sent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Final Rule expands scope beyond prenotification plans, the SBP recounts these historical disclosure requirements as the earlier Rule's specificity and as a point of comparison for the new, broader requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions added/clarified (e.g., 'material' and 'interactive electronic medium')
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule explicitly defines the terms 'material' and 'interactive electronic medium' consistent with their definitions and discussions in the NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions are included to clarify the scope of 'material' facts and the types of electronic media covered by the rule; they affect application of disclosure and consent obligations. The SBP notes the Commission added these definitions in response to comments for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to state laws (§425.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule states: "This part shall not be construed as superseding, altering, or affecting any State statute, regulation, order, or interpretation relating to negative option requirements, except to the extent it is inconsistent with the provisions of this part, and then only to the extent of the inconsistency."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal rule does not automatically preempt state laws; where inconsistent, the federal rule controls only to the extent of the inconsistency. Sellers must consider both federal and applicable state requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and severability (§425.8 and §425.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Rule adds a provision allowing requests for exemptions from the Final Rule consistent with the Commission's Rules of Practice and adds a severability provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision on exemptions allows regulated parties to seek relief under established Commission procedures. Severability clarifies that invalidation of one provision does not necessarily nullify the whole rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Billing without express informed consent is an unfair act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission reiterates that billing consumers without express informed consent is an unfair act under the FTC Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a core enforcement posture: merchants should not charge consumers without first obtaining express, informed authorization. The SBP ties this principle to the express informed consent requirement of §425.5 and to historical FTC enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed but not adopted provisions (annual reminders; pre-consent to receives 'saves')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission proposed (but did not adopt at this time) requirements for (1) annual reminders to consumers about negative option features and (2) prohibiting sellers from forcing consumers to receive 'saves' without first obtaining consumers' unambiguously affirmative consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission declined to adopt these two provisions in the final Rule, explaining it will seek further comment through a supplemental NPRM (SNPRM) and keeps the record open on these issues. These items thus reflect proposals under consideration but are not current compliance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and procedural requirements for promulgation (SBP under Magnuson-Moss / Section 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: To promulgate the rule under section 18 of the FTC Act (Magnuson-Moss), the Commission must issue a Statement of Basis and Purpose addressing: (a) prevalence of the acts/practices treated by the rule, (b) the manner/context they are unfair or deceptive, and (c) the economic effect of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural/legal standard governs the rulemaking process and shapes the analytical basis the Commission provides for the substantive obligations in the Rule (used by courts reviewing the rule). The SBP contains the required statements and economic analyses.
